profiles.meeting_scenario: A fortnightly coordination meeting between the NHS community frailty service and the local authority adult social care interface team in an English integrated care system, held one week before a revised case-management pathway goes live for community-dwelling adults aged 65 and over with moderate to severe frailty referred from GP practices, urgent community response, or hospital discharge. The meeting is focused on aligning routine handoffs rather than redesigning the pathway: how referral turnaround time will be interpreted on the dashboard, what counts as the required assessment within five working days, what artifact is meant by the shared care plan after the weekly frailty MDT, and what level of detail should be entered when MDT actions are recorded. Agenda: confirm go-live readiness, align intake and first-review workflow, confirm documentation expectations after MDT, and ensure both teams can produce consistent status updates in the first month. Expected outcome: both participants leave believing they have a common understanding of response-time reporting, assessment timing, shared documentation, and how MDT actions will be captured for follow-through.

members.name: Sarah Malik
members.role: Community Frailty Matron and Clinical Operations Lead
members.expertise: Community geriatric nursing, hospital avoidance pathways, multidisciplinary frailty assessment
members.background: Sarah is a senior nurse leading the neighbourhood frailty case-management service across two primary care networks; she previously ran a virtual ward pathway and is used to NHS operational dashboards, rapid clinical triage, and care planning inside the community EPR.
members.private_state: She wants the new pathway to look responsive in its first month, avoid unsafe delays after discharge, and keep the nursing team from being pulled into duplicate administrative work that does not change direct patient care.
hidden_assumptions: When people talk about referral turnaround time or time from acceptance, they mean the established operational clock that starts once a clinician has screened the referral as appropriate for the frailty caseload.
The five-day assessment standard is satisfied by the first substantive clinical review that identifies immediate risks and next steps, even if the fuller home-based review follows later.
A shared care plan can still be 'shared' when one team maintains the source clinical document and others work from the circulated MDT summary and action list.

Recording MDT actions means documenting clinically relevant decisions, key next steps, and any immediate risks clearly enough for professionals to act without turning the note into a task-management log.

members.name: Tom Bennett
members.expertise: Local authority care coordination, reablement handoffs, integrated discharge and community brokerage
members.background: Tom manages the social care coordinators embedded in the neighbourhood frailty team and is responsible for making sure the joint model interfaces cleanly with local authority workflows, cross-agency reporting, and follow-up on practical support actions.
members.private_state: He wants the integrated model to visibly function as a single front door, make social care actions visible early, and avoid his coordinators receiving vague MDT outputs that require extra chasing to turn into workable tasks.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss referral turnaround time or time from acceptance, they mean from the point the person is logged into the integrated pathway and visible on the joint tracker, because that is when the service has effectively received them.
The five-day assessment standard refers to the full initial holistic review that is usable for coordination, including function, home circumstances, carers, and immediate support needs.
A shared care plan implies one live cross-agency action-oriented artifact that each workstream can rely on directly, not a clinical source note plus downstream communication.

Recording MDT actions means entering explicit owners, due dates, and practical follow-up steps so that coordinators can progress equipment, brokerage, transport, and package-of-care items without interpretation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to keep referral turnaround time tight and to review performance as time from acceptance on the first-month dashboard.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the clock starts when a nurse or clinician has triaged the referral as suitable for the frailty caseload and opened it for active management.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the clock starts when the referral is logged onto the joint pathway tracker and treated as received by the integrated service.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like an existing reporting convention rather than a fresh design choice, so both assume the underlying timestamp is already settled somewhere in operational guidance and do not pause to define it.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the five-day assessment
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the person should have their assessment within five working days so the pathway feels responsive.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this is met by an initial nurse-led clinical assessment by phone or in person covering urgent symptoms, medication issues, red flags, and whether escalation or a home visit is needed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this is met only by a fuller holistic assessment, usually home-based, that includes mobility, daily functioning, home environment, carer strain, and current support arrangements.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same pathway phrase and both genuinely support prompt assessment; each defaults to the version embedded in their own reporting culture, making the difference feel too obvious to mention.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of the shared care plan
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the shared care plan should be updated after the Wednesday frailty MDT so everyone is working from the same plan.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means updating the clinical care-plan template in the NHS community record and distributing the agreed MDT summary so partner teams can see the latest plan.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means maintaining a jointly usable cross-agency plan that directly contains the actions social care coordinators and health staff will work from.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word 'shared' creates a strong sense of common understanding, and both care about cross-team visibility; neither expects that they disagree about whether sharing means common access to one authoritative document or coordinated use of linked artifacts.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to capture MDT actions
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree Sarah's team will capture the MDT actions after the huddle so nothing gets missed.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes her team will enter a concise professional note listing decisions, key actions, and any risk-related follow-up, trusting each discipline to translate relevant items into its own workflow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes Sarah's team will record actions in a task-ready format with named owners, expected timing, and enough practical detail for direct handoff to coordinators.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At the surface level both are simply agreeing that actions will be documented promptly; the hidden divergence is about granularity and task structure, which usually feels like an obvious matter of professional note-taking rather than something to negotiate.

turns.inner_thought: We are close enough to go-live that I need this kept practical. I do not want today turning into a redesign conversation. What matters is that the pathway looks responsive in the first month, especially for post-discharge patients, and that my nurses are not dragged into duplicate admin that adds nothing to care.
turns.utterance: Thanks, Tom. I wanted to use today just to make sure next Monday's frailty case-management go-live is operationally smooth across intake, first review, and MDT follow-through, so we're not trying to fix basic handoffs in week one.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to present as one integrated front door from day one. If a person is on the joint tracker, the pathway has effectively received them, and that is where the clock should feel real. The dashboard wording matters because governance will read it as evidence that integration is or is not functioning.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. My main concern is that from day one it feels like a single front door rather than two separate processes, and that referral turnaround time reads clearly on the dashboard.

turns.inner_thought: That should be fine if we're talking about the usual operational clock from acceptance after clinical screening into the frailty caseload. We already review accepted cases every morning, and urgent ones can be moved through fast. I do not want performance judged from the point something lands before anyone has established whether it belongs with us.
turns.utterance: I think that should look fine. Once cases are accepted, we'll review them each morning, and anything urgent can be moved quickly onto the caseload, so referral turnaround time ought to stay tight.

turns.inner_thought: Good. For me, acceptance means once they're logged and visible on the integrated pathway tracker. Governance colleagues will look closely at post-discharge flow and want to see the elapsed time from that point through to assessment, without gaps where nobody can tell what is happening.
turns.utterance: That's reassuring. Governance colleagues will especially watch time from acceptance to assessment for post-discharge referrals in the first month, so it helps if we can show that moving cleanly.

turns.inner_thought: The five-day standard is manageable because the duty nurse can do the first substantive clinical review quickly, by phone or in person, even if home-visit capacity is tight. If we cover urgent symptoms, medication issues, red flags, and immediate next steps, that is responsive and safe.
turns.utterance: Yes, the person should have their assessment within five working days so the pathway feels responsive, and that should be manageable because the duty nurse can complete an assessment promptly even when home-visit capacity is tight.

turns.inner_thought: As long as that assessment gives a usable holistic picture, we are fine. My coordinators need to understand home circumstances, carers, and what support is already in place early on, otherwise they are stuck chasing context before they can move anything practical.
turns.utterance: That should help, yes, as long as the assessment gives enough early clarity on home circumstances, carers, and what's already in place, so coordination can get going without too much delay.

turns.inner_thought: On documentation, I want this anchored in the community clinical record. In my mind the shared care plan is the care-plan template we update after the frailty MDT, with the MDT summary circulated so everyone has the latest agreed position. That is shared enough without creating another live document for my team to maintain.
turns.utterance: On the documentation side, the shared care plan should be updated after the Wednesday frailty MDT so everyone is working from the same plan.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly. If the shared care plan is current after Wednesday, my coordinators should be able to use that one live cross-agency plan directly for equipment, transport, and package-of-care work, without bouncing between separate notes and emails.
turns.utterance: Agreed. If the shared care plan is current after the Wednesday meeting, that should let my coordinators pick up equipment, transport, and package-of-care actions without chasing around.

turns.inner_thought: We can document promptly after the huddle, but I need to keep this proportionate. My team can enter a concise professional note with the decisions, key actions, and risk-related follow-up the same afternoon. I am not turning the MDT output into a detailed task-management log for every discipline.
turns.utterance: That's fine from our side. My team will capture the MDT actions after the huddle so nothing gets missed, and we can have the update out the same afternoon.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I am assuming 'capture the MDT actions' means actions are recorded in a task-ready way with enough clarity for coordinators to start immediately. If that happens, the social care side can move practical items without additional interpretation.
turns.utterance: That's really helpful, because once the MDT actions are captured, my coordinators should be able to start progressing the practical items straight away.

turns.inner_thought: A discharge example will reassure him without opening up a debate about what exactly counts as the five-day assessment. The point is that once the case is accepted onto the frailty caseload and clinically reviewed, we can act quickly on immediate risk like medicines and keep people safe.
turns.utterance: Just thinking of a recent discharge case, that's really how it worked in practice: once it was accepted and assessed, we could stabilise the medication issues quickly and stop things drifting. That's the sort of flow we want to preserve.

turns.inner_thought: I think we're aligned. As long as the joint front door is visible, the dashboard tells a clean story from acceptance, people are assessed within five days in a way that supports coordination, and the shared plan and actions are updated after MDT, I can tell the local authority side we're ready.
turns.utterance: Yes, that sounds workable to me. If we keep the front end tight, make sure people are seen within the five-day window, and keep the plan and follow-up current after the Wednesday huddle, I'm comfortable saying we're ready to go.
